item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports separating persistent preferences, immediate intent, and recurring interests. [MSMT-LSI (2024)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-024-00460-5) combines separate long- and short-term attention networks with multiple temporal embeddings. [Denoising Long- and Short-term Interests (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.14743) models session-level interest evolution and uses contrastive augmentation to reduce incidental-interaction noise. [MIMAR-SRec (2026)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/38489) learns intent representations across contextual windows, aligning sequences with intent prototypes while adding robustness to interaction and temporal noise.\n\nThe closest match is [HyperHawkes (WWW 2025)](https://evazangerle.at/publication/peintner-www-2025/): contrastive clustering extracts latent intents; Hawkes processes model recurring intent and long-term preferences; a multi-level attention mixture captures immediate interests. Its key implication: elapsed time need not imply monotonically declining relevance—some interests recur. An architecture hypothesis for this benchmark is a lightweight SASRec extension combining recent-context features, pooled historical preferences, and a small latent-intent bank through a learned gate conditioned on observed time gaps. Compare learned decay against a decay-plus-recurrence variant. Treat purchase saturation as an unverified hypothesis, not an observed satisfaction signal; histories alone do not establish why interest changed. Under unseen-item recommendation, intent recurrence can transfer to related unseen products even when exact-item repetition cannot contribute. These adaptations are proposals, not established gains on the pinned benchmark."}
